### Problem: Summary Ranges {#sec-tp-p6-a}

::: {.p-statement}
A sorted unique integer array $\mathit{nums}$ ($0 \le n \le 20$, $-2^{31} \le \mathit{nums}[i] \le 2^{31}-1$). The tiny $n$ means any correct method passes; the point is the linear group pointer, which is what larger versions of the problem need. Return the *minimal* list of ranges covering exactly the elements: a range $[a, b]$ with $a < b$ is written "a->b", a lone element $a$ is written "a", and consecutive elements must share a range wherever possible.

Source: [LC 228 · Summary Ranges](https://leetcode.com/problems/summary-ranges/){.solved difficulty="Easy"}
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
"Minimal" forces you to group: the array is already sorted, so a run is a maximal block where each step advances by exactly $1$. One pointer $\mathit{i}$ marks the start of the current run, a second pointer $\mathit{j}$ walks forward *while the chain holds* ($\mathit{nums}[j+1] = \mathit{nums}[j] + 1$), and when $\mathit{j}$ stops the whole run $[\mathit{i}, \mathit{j}]$ is emitted in one go and $\mathit{i}$ resumes from $\mathit{j}+1$. This is the group-pointer shape of @sec-tp-runs — $\mathit{j}$ never rewinds, so the two nested loops together still cost $O(n)$.
:::

::: {.p-approach}
1. **Membership via a set.** Put every value in a set; scan sorted values, start a range only at a run head ($x - 1$ absent) and stretch $y$ while $y + 1$ is present. $O(n\log n)$ for the sort — correct, but re-derives sortedness the input already gave you. The oracle.
2. **Group pointer over the sorted array.** $\mathit{i}$ holds the run start, $\mathit{j}$ jumps the whole chain, emit, continue at $\mathit{j}+1$. $O(n)$, $O(1)$ extra beyond the output.

**Invariant.** At the top of each outer iteration, $\mathit{i}$ is the first index of a not-yet-emitted run, and $\mathit{j}$ has advanced exactly while consecutive-value chains hold — so $[\mathit{i}, \mathit{j}]$ is a *maximal* run and minimality is preserved.
:::

The buttons are in order. Each one keeps the previous solution and changes only what that form changes.

::: {.panel-tabset .solution-forms}

#### Stretch each run from a set

::: {.form-next}
Treat it as a membership problem: sort the values into a set, and for each potential run head extend while successors exist. $O(n\log n)$ time. Written first because it is obviously correct from the definition of "range", which makes it a fair oracle — and it also handles an unsorted input, which the refined version deliberately does not.

**"Set", in plain words.** A `set` is a bag of distinct values that answers "is $x$ in it?" in $O(1)$ (the hash-set idea of @sec-hash-sets). Here we exploit that to test membership of neighbours: a value $x$ *starts* a run exactly when $x-1$ is **not** present, and the run ends at the largest $y$ reachable by repeatedly finding $y+1$ present.

**Worked example.** nums $= [0, 1, 2, 4, 5, 7]$, so $s = \{0, 1, 2, 4, 5, 7\}$. Walking sorted values: $0$ starts a run ($-1 \notin s$) and stretches $0\to1\to2$ (since $3 \notin s$) → "0->2"; $1$ and $2$ are skipped (their predecessor is present, so they aren't heads); $4$ starts a run stretching to $5$ ($6 \notin s$) → "4->5"; $7$ is alone → "7". Result `["0->2", "4->5", "7"]`.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
def summary_ranges_brute(nums):
    s = set(nums); res = []
    for x in sorted(s):
        if x - 1 in s:
            continue                    # not a run head; the head will emit it
        y = x
        while y + 1 in s:
            y += 1
        res.append(f"{x}" if x == y else f"{x}->{y}")
    return res
```

##### C++

```cpp
// fragment - set-based oracle
#include <vector>
#include <set>
#include <string>
using namespace std;
vector<string> summaryRangesBrute(vector<int> nums) {
    set<int> s(nums.begin(), nums.end());
    vector<string> res;
    for (int x : s) {
        if (s.count(x - 1)) continue;
        int y = x;
        while (s.count(y + 1)) ++y;
        res.push_back(x == y ? to_string(x)
                              : to_string(x) + "->" + to_string(y));
    }
    return res;
}
```
:::

**Reading it line by line.** `s = set(nums)` gives $O(1)$ membership tests and drops duplicates, so we work with the distinct values. `for x in sorted(s)` visits them in increasing order. `if x - 1 in s: continue` is the run-head test — if the value just below $x$ exists, some earlier $x$ already opened this run, so we skip and let the head emit it. Otherwise `y = x` then `while y + 1 in s: y += 1` stretches rightward as far as consecutive values allow, and `res.append(f"{x}" if x == y else f"{x}->{y}")` writes a lone number or an arrow range. The re-sorting (`sorted(s)`) is the $O(n\log n)$ we pay for not trusting the input's order.

#### Group pointer that jumps a run

::: {.form-next}
Drop the set and use the sorted order directly: $\mathit{j}$ races ahead through the chain of consecutive values while $\mathit{nums}[j+1] = \mathit{nums}[j] + 1$ holds, the pair $(\mathit{i}, \mathit{j})$ describes the whole run, and $\mathit{i}$ restarts at $\mathit{j} + 1$. One pass, and the inner steps are charged to $\mathit{j}$'s monotone walk.

**Worked example.** nums $= [0, 1, 2, 4, 5, 7]$. $\mathit{i}=0$: $\mathit{j}$ races $0\to1\to2$ (stops before $4$, since $4 \ne 2+1$), emit "0->2", set $\mathit{i}=3$. $\mathit{i}=3$ (value $4$): $\mathit{j}$ races to $4$ (value $5$), stops before index $5$ (value $7\ne5+1$), emit "4->5", $\mathit{i}=5$. $\mathit{i}=5$ (value $7$): $\mathit{j}$ can't move, $\mathit{i}=\mathit{j}$ so emit "7". Same `["0->2", "4->5", "7"]`, no set and no sort.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false

def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("summary", "runs")
    assert str(final) == "['0->2', '4->5', '7']"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
#| label: arr-summary-ranges
def summary_ranges(nums):
    res = []; i = 0; n = len(nums)
    while i < n:
        j = i
        while j + 1 < n and nums[j + 1] == nums[j] + 1:
            j += 1                      # jump one more chained element
        res.append(f"{nums[i]}" if i == j else f"{nums[i]}->{nums[j]}")
        i = j + 1                       # next run starts right after this one
    return res

for _ in range(300):
    nums = sorted(set(random.randint(0, 15) for _ in range(random.randint(0, 9))))
    assert summary_ranges(nums) == summary_ranges_brute(nums)
assert summary_ranges([0, 1, 2, 4, 5, 7]) == ["0->2", "4->5", "7"]   # LC sample
assert summary_ranges([0, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 9]) == ["0", "2->4", "6", "8->9"]
assert summary_ranges([-1]) == ["-1"]
assert summary_ranges([]) == []
print("summary_ranges OK")
```

##### C++

```cpp
#include <vector>
#include <string>
using namespace std;

class Solution {
public:
    vector<string> summaryRanges(const vector<int>& nums) {
        vector<string> res;
        int n = (int)nums.size();
        for (int i = 0; i < n; ) {
            int j = i;
            while (j + 1 < n && (long long)nums[j + 1] == (long long)nums[j] + 1) ++j;
            string head = to_string(nums[i]);
            res.push_back(i == j ? head : head + "->" + to_string(nums[j]));
            i = j + 1;
        }
        return res;
    }
};
```
:::

**Reading it line by line.** `i = 0` marks the start of the current run; `j = i` starts a second finger that will race ahead. The inner `while j + 1 < n and nums[j + 1] == nums[j] + 1: j += 1` keeps jumping forward only while the chain of consecutive integers holds, so when it stops $[\mathit{i}, \mathit{j}]$ is a *maximal* run. `res.append(f"{nums[i]}" if i == j else f"{nums[i]}->{nums[j]}")` emits a lone value when the run has one element ($\mathit{i}=\mathit{j}$) and an arrow otherwise. `i = j + 1` starts the next run immediately after this one. Because $\mathit{j}$ only ever moves forward and $\mathit{i}$ jumps to $\mathit{j}+1$, the two loops together touch each element once — $O(n)$, not $O(n^2)$.

:::

::: {.p-complexity}
**Stretch each run from a set** is $O(n\log n)$ time (for the sort) and $O(n)$ space. **Group pointer that jumps a run** is $O(n)$ time — the inner `while` advances $\mathit{j}$, and $\mathit{j}$ is re-set to $\mathit{i} \ge$ old $\mathit{j} + 1$, so the total number of inner steps across the whole run is $\le n$ (the charging argument of @sec-tp-runs) — plus $O(1)$ extra space. Output size is $\le n$ strings either way.
:::

::: {.p-edge}
- $\mathit{nums}[j] = 2^{31} - 1$ at the top of the int range: `nums[j] + 1` overflows in C++ `int` — widen to `long long` in the chain test, as above (Python integers make this invisible, @sec-arr-cost).
- $n = 0$ returns `[]` — the outer loop never runs, so there is no special case to write.
- A lone run ($i = j$) emits just "a", never "a->a"; LC explicitly disallows single-element arrow ranges.
:::

- @sec-tp-p6-b (CF 1343C, Alternating Subsequence) — the same group pointer, but the chain test is "same sign" instead of "next value", and each run contributes its maximum.
